newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - INSTANT VIEW - Australian August imports data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - INSTANT VIEW - Australian August imports data.

text.p: Australian imports rose by one percent in August, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said.
Economists' median forecast had been for a 2.2 percent rise, with forecasts ranging from a 1.0 percent fall to a 5.0 percent rise.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follow.
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"I think it's probably at the soft end of expectations. The number suggests the current account (deficit) will be probably pretty similar to last month, probably around the A$1.3 billion mark. It still indicates...that the tone of econonic activity is still softish. Clearly we got a biggish rise in consumer goods imports. The trend there has been flat to negative over the past three months. Capital goods came back a bit, but that's after two very big falls and that does include that Qantas aircraft, and coupled with the decline in intermediates, it still suggests to me that the tone of private spending is still pretty soft."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, STATE BANK OF NSW:

"We'd be looking at about A$1.35-1.4 billion (current account deficit). The big story for us is that imports remain soft, it's a reflection of a soft economy, and we think the Reserve Bank will have to move on monetary policy before Christmas just to get the place going again."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"They were a bit softer than I thought they would be. I was looking for a bit more of a rebound, especially after the weakness we have seen in recent months. It will tend to keep alive market expectations of monetary policy easing after the November Reserve Bank board meeting as it suggests that economic activity is still in a somewhat softer patch."
DAVID BASSANESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BT AUSTRALIA:

"If you exclude aircraft capital imports have fallen in the last four months, part of that is the price effect (of the Australian dollar's appreciation). It's just generally consistent with the slow patch in the economy. Current account deficit forecast - A$1.2 billion, another good number with a bounceback in exports in all probability.

"On the surface, the market should take the data quite positively. It seems to suggest the economy is relatively soft. But we would be cautious as we think capital imports will pick up over the coming months."
